articles.title: Xi hails Russia ties as ‘source of stability’ ahead of trilateral summit
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: The Chinese President opened the two-day APEC gathering with an address to a CEO Summit, where he made a pitch for openness and stable supply chains

Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday hailed relations with Russia “as a source of stability” in a “turbulent” world, even as he welcomed U.S. President Donald Trump with a rare airport reception a day ahead of a trilateral summit in Shenzhen.

On Thursday (November 19, 2026), leaders of the three countries will hold a summit, which Beijing has described as having “groundbreaking significance”. U.S. officials said the three leaders will likely discuss, among other issues, the war in Ukraine, the situation in Iran, global energy stability, and nuclear arms control.

Officials have described the rare trilateral leaders’ summit as more of an exploratory and symbolic meeting, playing down the likelihood of substantive outcomes, either with regard to a possible Russia-Ukraine deal or on the West Asian crisis. Whether they can see eye-to-eye on nuclear disarmament also remains to be seen.
At the same time, Beijing has highlighted the symbolism of the summit happening on its soil, describing it as a landmark moment for what China calls “major country diplomacy”.

In talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday (November 18, 2026), Mr. Xi described China-Russia relations “as a source of stability and certainty in a turbulent world and as a model of a new type of major-power relationship characterised by equality, mutual respect, trust, and win-win cooperation.”

The U.S. President landed in Shenzhen on Wednesday (November 18, 2026), and Mr. Xi welcomed him at the airport with a hug — a rare greeting from the Chinese President, who was reciprocating Mr. Trump similarly receiving him in September at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington.

Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomes US President Donald Trump as he arrives at Shenzhen Airport to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders Summit in Shenzhen, China on November 18, 2026. | Photo Credit: Reuters
The Chinese President opened the two-day APEC gathering with an address to a CEO Summit, where he made a pitch for openness and stable supply chains.

“The world is facing mounting instability, insufficient momentum for economic growth, and a resurgence of unilateralism and protectionism. At the same time, global trade is still growing despite headwinds and emerging technologies are advancing rapidly, reshaping global development,” he said, adding that “the key questions of the age were whether the world would choose openness or closure, cooperation or division, reform or stagnation.”

Mr. Xi called for barriers to trade and investment to be reduced and proposed establishing a World Bay Area Economic Cooperation Alliance. Beijing has been developing the Greater Bay Area, including Shenzhen, Hong Kong and Macau, as an innovation hub.

His remarks came amid continuing China-U.S. trade tensions over a number of issues, including semiconductors and rare earths. Both sides have so far only agreed to extend their trade truce until January, while they continue working on other unresolved issues.

China's President Xi Jinping, right, welcomes President Donald Trump as he arrives at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport in Shenzhen in southern China's Guangdong Province, on November 18, 2026. | Photo Credit: AP

articles.title: Scientists warn of growing health threats of chemicals found everywhere
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: EDCs are chemicals that interfere with, mimic, or block the hormones that regulate the development and behaviour of our organs
Chemicals found almost everywhere in modern life pose a "global and growing threat" to human health and the environment, a landmark report based on over a decade of research has warned.

The report on "endocrine-disrupting chemicals" (EDCs) released by the United Nations Environment Programme and World Health Organization "conservatively" estimates the health and environmental costs of EDC exposure at over $1 trillion annually.

"The scientific evidence is clear: EDCs are a global and growing threat to human and environmental health," warns the report written by international scientists, calling current regulations "uneven and insufficient."
EDCs are chemicals that interfere with, mimic, or block the hormones that regulate the development and behaviour of our organs.
They are in everything from toys and makeup, to building materials and clothing.
The report released late Tuesday is the first such comprehensive look at EDC impacts in 14 years, and finds increasingly clear links between them and a range of diseases.
"The evidence is so strong that it's irrefutable at this point," said Laura Vandenberg, report co-author and professor of environmental health sciences at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.
The report examined thousands of studies on chemicals like bisphenols, phthalates and parabens.
Evidence of links between these chemicals and disease is strongest for certain neurological conditions and reproductive problems including sperm decline.
But there is also growing confidence that EDCs are linked to diseases like type 2 diabetes and asthma that have spiked globally.
"Because these changes are occurring rapidly, they are unlikely to be explained primarily by genetic change," the report says.
Scientists looked at associations between EDC exposure and health conditions, as well as the mechanisms by which exposure could cause harm.

articles.title: Researchers boost gut microbial activity linked to longevity in aged mice, find improved metabolism
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: The study suggests that specific age-related changes in the gut microbiome may be protective adaptations rather than signs of decline, and could potentially be harnessed to support healthier ageing

Researchers have identified changes in the metabolic activity of the gut microbiome associated with exceptional longevity in humans, and found that amplifying the same activity in aged mice using engineered bacteria improved metabolic health.

Published in the journal Cell Metabolism , the team's study suggests that specific age-related changes in the gut microbiome may be protective adaptations rather than signs of decline, and could potentially be harnessed to support healthier aging.

Senior author Amir Zarrinpar, chair in circadian biology and medicine, and professor of medicine at the University of California San Diego, said while many studies on aging focus on what goes wrong as one grows old, the findings suggest "some changes in the gut microbiome may actually represent the body's attempt to preserve metabolic health".
"If we can identify those beneficial functions and safely strengthen them, we may eventually be able to develop new ways to promote healthier aging," Zarrinpar said.

The gut microbiome, the community of bacteria and other microbes living in the digestive tract, is known to change throughout life and plays an important role in metabolism and inflammation, among other aspects of health.
Studies have also found distinctive microbiome features among people who age exceptionally well.
The researchers focused on how gut microbes modify bile acids, substances produced by the liver that help digest fats but also act as signalling molecules in the body.

Studying young and aged mice, they found that aging was associated with an increased microbial activity linked to enzymes called bile salt hydrolases. These enzymes chemically modify bile acids, allowing them to influence pathways involved in metabolism, inflammation and the body's internal clock.
The team also found greater bile acid modification in the mice.
To determine patterns in humans, they reanalysed publicly available data from a human ageing cohort, analysing bile acid measurements from 48 young adults, 107 older adults and 125 centenarians.

The centenarian group showed higher ratios of modified bile acids than both younger groups. An analysis of microbiome data also revealed a greater abundance of a gene associated with bile salt hydrolase activity among centenarians compared with the older adult group.
Further, aged mice -- 82-week-old mice -- were introduced with a strain of bacteria native to the gut engineered to continuously produce bile salt hydrolases.

articles.title: Does India need to financially aid families’ decisions to have a child through fertility treatment?
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: Indian laws protect the decision not to have a child through statutes, schemes and subsidies, but the decision to have one is left to the mercy of the private assisted reproduction healthcare market

The reproductive-autonomy jurisprudence as evolved by the Supreme Court under Article 21 of the Constitution is rich yet narrow, focusing primarily on one side of the problem. In Suchita Srivastava v. Chandigarh Administration (2009), the Court held that reproductive choices may be exercised to procreate as well as to abstain from procreating. In X v. Principal Secretary, Health and Family Welfare Department (2022), the Supreme Court extended the right to abortion to unmarried women as an exercise of ‘decisional autonomy’.

These, and nearly all other landmark cases are concerned only with an existing pregnancy. The freedom to pursue parenthood through medical treatment, however, has surfaced only at the margins. The Delhi High Court, in 2023, allowed parole of a life convict to attempt IVF, by recognising a “right to parenthood,” but only as a claim against a barrier the State itself had erected. No court has yet asked whether the State may leave a citizen’s access to infertility care entirely to their own purse. Can a right available to the fertile but structurally withheld from the infertile be called a universal right?

Science, Space & Environment Report: Does India need to financially aid families’ decisions to have a child through fertility treatment?. This milestone highlights indigenous research, technological self-reliance, and environmental sustainability.

Scientific & Technical Core: Innovations led by ISRO, DRDO, CSIR, and national research institutes are advancing India's capabilities in space exploration, quantum computing, biotechnology, and clean energy.

No court has yet asked whether the State may leave a citizen’s access to infertility care entirely to their own purse. Can a right available to the fertile but structurally withheld from the infertile be called a universal right?

Principal Secretary, Health and Family Welfare Department (2022), the Supreme Court extended the right to abortion to unmarried women as an exercise of ‘decisional autonomy’.

articles.title: India imposes 162.5% duty and tax on bulk Scotch imports amid UK trade pact dispute
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: More than 80 containers belonging to Pernod Ricard, Diageo and Bacardi remain stuck at Indian ports as the dispute over customs classification threatens to disrupt the liquor industry.

India is imposing an effective duty of 162.5% on bulk Scotch imports amid an ongoing dispute over the India-UK trade agreement, raising concerns among liquor companies as the levy exceeds the 150% charged before the agreement, according to eight sources and a government document.

The India-UK trade agreement, implemented in July, halved tariffs on Scotch to 75%. Businesses and the British government had hailed the move as a major win for companies such as Pernod Ricard and Diageo, which import Scotch in bulk and blend it to make popular products for India’s USD 65-billion liquor market.

However, in the first major dispute linked to the trade agreement, Indian investigators have argued that companies are using incorrect customs classifications for bulk Scotch concentrates, which are treated as raw materials used to make drinks such as blended whiskies.

Since May, such imports have been classified under a newly created customs category for “compound alcoholic preparations”, which attracts a 150% t tariff, according to Indian investigators. These imports are then subject to a consumption tax, taking the total duty to 162.5% , according to a government document reviewed by Reuters and eight sources, including industry executives and customs agents familiar with the matter.
As the dispute continues, thousands of litres of bulk Scotch in more than 80 shipping containers belonging to Pernod, Diageo and Bacardi remain stuck at ports, Reuters reported last week.
Under a provisional release arrangement pending investigation, 75% of the goods’ value must be paid upfront, with the remaining amount covered by bank guarantees, the sources said.

“Industry has already reduced prices of Scotch products in the market when the India-UK pact kicked in, and now they are faced with higher duties again,” said a source in the liquor importing business.
Pernod, which owns UK-based Chivas Brothers, Diageo and several other Indian companies believe that both bulk and bottled Scotch imports should be taxed at 75% under the trade agreement.
The British government has repeatedly said in statements that it is working with New Delhi to resolve the issue, while India has said the dispute will be settled soon.

Pernod and Diageo have moved to arrange bank guarantees and other funding to secure the release of their blocked containers and ensure business continuity. Bacardi is still deciding its next steps, three of the sources said.

Shares of Diageo in London and Pernod in France fell following the Reuters report, declining 1.5% and 1.25%, respectively. India is Pernod’s biggest global market by volume, and the company, along with Diageo, dominates the Indian spirits market.
Diageo declined to comment, while Pernod and Bacardi did not respond to queries. The Indian Finance Ministry and the tax authority also did not respond.

articles.title: India, Canada eye defence pact during Modi visit in December
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: India’s High Commissioner to Ottawa says both countries cannot afford to let fringe issues derail their extensive mutual interests
India and Canada could be announcing a defence agreement during Prime Minister Narendra Modi ’s official visit in December, according to the country’s High Commissioner to Ottawa, Dinesh K. Patnaik.
Both countries are also in the final stages of negotiations of a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement. “We are on the cusp of finalising it,” Mr. Patnaik said.

Addressing a gathering in the Canadian capital organised by the Centre for Strategic Statecraft and the Canadian International Council, he said that both countries cannot afford to let fringe issues derail their extensive mutual interests.

Mr. Patnaik took over as India’s High Commissioner to Ottawa in September 2025. Both countries had earlier expelled each other’s High Commissioners and reduced their diplomatic presence following the murder of Sikh Khalistani activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in June 2023. Then Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau accused India of orchestrating the murder, throwing bilateral relations into a tailspin. Subsequent reports by Canadian agencies also listed India, alongside China and Russia, as an interferer in domestic politics. The turnaround in ties, which began with the mutual reinstatement of High Commissioners, is set to reach a milestone with Mr. Modi’s visit on December 11 and 12.

Mr. Patnaik said India and Canada are no longer talking about a reset of their derailed relations, but rather an overarching boost in ties spanning defence, space, nuclear energy, deep tech, trade, and the mobility of people. The two nations have moved from a complete lack of trust over a year ago to an unprecedented degree of mutual trust, he added.

“The fact is that in the core strategic concerns of Canada and India, there is no conflict. Still, all it took for the entire bilateral relationship to be derailed was the fringe diaspora issue,” he said, referring to the murder of Nijjar.

“The reason was the lack of trust. India believed that Canada was actively promoting separatism in India, and Canada believed India was organising violence in Canada. We had a series of meetings between senior Ministers, NSAs of both countries, and agencies at all levels as we set about rebuilding trust. Today, we have reached the highest levels of trust, where the most sensitive areas of cooperation, such as deep tech, defence, and space, are subjects of mutual cooperation,” Mr. Patnaik said.
Cooperation between Canadian and Indian agencies remains at a high level, the High Commissioner added.

articles.title: Bengaluru is India’s AI, start-up capital; city captures 47% of national venture funding
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The city is now the world’s fifth-largest unicorn hub, the largest outside the U.S., Europe, and China, with 57 unicorns valued at $211 billion, representing 55.3% of the combined value of all Indian unicorns
City-based start-ups have raised about $85 billion since 2010, 47% of all venture funding raised by Indian start-ups, with $76.5 billion of it in the past 10 years.

This milestone was revealed in the Bengaluru Innovation Report 2026, released on Wednesday (November 18, 2026) by Karnataka’s Minister for Home, Electronics, IT & BT, Priyank M. Kharge, during the second day of the Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026.
Prepared by the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission (KDEM) and 3one4 Capital, using Tracxn data, the report highlights the city’s evolution into a global deep-tech powerhouse.

According to the findings, Bengaluru is unequivocally India’s Artificial Intelligence capital, commanding 36.3% of the country’s native AI start-up funding and housing 71% of India’s AI and deep-tech unicorns created since 2023. Out of 1,556 deep-tech startups founded in the city since 2010, 1,319 are active and funded, raising $3.77 billion. Women entrepreneurs are also driving this wave, with nearly 30% of India’s active, funded women-led deep-tech and AI start-ups originating in the city, raising $323.65 million.

The city’s wealth creation metrics remain unmatched nationally. Bengaluru is now the world’s fifth-largest unicorn hub, and the largest outside the US, Europe, and China, with 57 unicorns valued at $211 billion, representing 55.3% of the combined value of all Indian unicorns.

Further, as per the report, it leads the nation with 212 “soonicorns” (soon-to-be unicorns). Start-ups here scale faster than anywhere else in India, reaching unicorn status in six years and public exits in 8.2 years, beating the global exit average of 11.1 years. Since November 2024, 16 Bengaluru-linked companies have gone public with a combined listing value of $42 billion.

Mr. Kharge emphasised on expanding this success across the State. “The Bengaluru Innovation Report 2026 shows how far Karnataka’s founders have come and how much more they can build from here. Our next task is to make sure a world-class AI, quantum or semiconductor company can grow just as well in Kalaburagi, Hubballi or Mangaluru. Deep tech rewards patience, and Karnataka will stay the course,’’ he stated.

The State is backing this vision with aggressive regional initiatives, including the ₹1,000 crore Local Economy Accelerator Programme (LEAP), Global Technology Centres in Mysuru, Hubballi, and Belagavi, and the ELEVATE grant programme, which has already supported 1,479 start-ups across 30 districts.

Highlighting the ecosystem’s investor appeal, KDEM chairman B.V. Naidu, a key architect of Karnataka’s IT industry, noted, “This report gives investors, GCCs and founders a data-backed view of what Karnataka, Bengaluru and our emerging clusters, offers.’’
Through the Beyond Bengaluru Mission, BLUE investor days and the Cluster Seed Fund, KDEM would keep connecting capital and companies with talent across the State, Mr. Naidu added.

KEONICS chairman Sharath Bachegowda concluded that through continued investments in infrastructure and talent, the state aims to build an ecosystem where enterprises “can innovate, scale and compete globally”.

Industry and government leaders echoed the shift toward homegrown capital, noting that 52% of Alternative Investment Fund (AIF) capital now comes from domestic investors. “With 36.3% of India’s native AI funding already in Bengaluru, the next decade belongs to founders building hard technology for the world from Karnataka,” opined Prashant Prakash, chairman of Karnataka’s Vision Group on Startups.

articles.title: Dalits in Gorakhpur face more injustice than anywhere else, alleges Akhilesh
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: If polls were held today, BJP would face “double-zero” defeat in CM’s home constituency, says SP chief; says 26,000 primary schools in U.P. shut over last 10 years; vows to provide AIIMS-level facilities in government hospitals

Alleging that Dalits in Gorakhpur face more injustice than anywhere else, Samajwadi Party president Akhilesh Yadav said on Wednesday that the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) would face a “double-zero” defeat on Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath’s home turf if elections were held today.

“There is tremendous enthusiasm among the people of Gorakhpur for change. If voting happens today, BJP will become double zero in Gorakhpur just like Kashi,” he said. The Assembly election is not just about winning seats, but about the future of the State and its people. The Assembly election is an election to save democracy. It is an election for the right to vote. If injustice is being done to Dalits anywhere, then it is happening the most in Gorakhpur,” he added, after unveiling a statue of the revolutionary figure Babu Bandhu Singh in Devkahi, in the Chauri Chaura Assembly constituency in Gorakhpur.
The SP chief promised to provide All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS)-like facilities in other government medical colleges in the region.

“Here in the medical college, children died due to lack of oxygen. If anyone helped those children, it was the Samajwadi Party. The government hospitals here are not providing the treatment they should, and the poor are still facing extortion. In the coming times, facilities like AIIMS will be available in medical colleges as well. If a Samajwadi government is formed, you will not have to show any card,” he promised.

Reiterating his slogan, ‘Haata Nahi Bhaata’, the SP chief promised to establish social justice by forming a PDA government, an acronym for the voting bloc of minorities, Dalits, and other backward classes.

“We will establish social justice by forming a PDA government. We will build a nation of brothers. We will honor our immortal martyrs and revolutionaries and bring respect to society,” he said, accusing the BJP government of betraying farmers and youth over the last 10 years. “They have ruined their future. The public has witnessed BJP’s 10 years of rule. We hope that the people of Gorakhpur will win all seats for the Samajwadi Party... We will establish the rule of law. There will be no discrimination against anyone,” added Mr. Yadav.

He alleged that in 10 years of the BJP government, 26,000 primary schools have been closed down in Uttar Pradesh. “And when I looked back and calculated where all the schools have been shut down, do you know how many schools have been closed in your Gorakhpur? Approximately 500 schools have been closed down in your area,” he said.

Earlier, from the Gorakhpur airport, Mr. Yadav boarded the PDA Rath, a specially designed vehicle. He reached Devkahi village in Chauri Chaura through a roadshow with a huge crowd of SP workers that gathered to welcome him on the route from the airport to the village.

The SP said the issues raised by Mr. Yadav — including atrocities against Dalits, the closure of primary schools, lack of facilities in AIIMS, discrimination against Brahmins — resonated with the public.

“The 20 km roadshow with cheering crowds and several well-attended programmes in Gorakhpur is to convince the people of Uttar Pradesh that the Samajwadi Party is going to win the 2027 Assembly election,” said senior SP leader Sudhir Panwar. “The strategy behind challenging the Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath at his home turf is a calculated move to send a strong message to the public and BJP leaders that the political stature of Akhilesh Yadav ji is far above the State leadership. The issues raised by Akhilesh Yadav on atrocities against Dalits, closure of primary schools, lack of facilities in AIIMS, discrimination against Brahmins find resonance with the public,” he added.

articles.title: Introduce age-appropriate awareness programmes for school students in academics over trafficking, commercial sexual exploitation: HC to government
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: High Court bench says that there should not be any delay in referring complaints relating to online sexual exploitation, intimate images or suspected child sexual abuse material to the competent police officer or cybercrime official

The Telangana High Court on Wednesday passed a slew of instructions to top officials of different wings of State government, including the Director General of Police, over rescue and rehabilitation of women and children rescued from trafficking and commercial sexual exploitation.

In one of the directions, the HC said ‘under no circumstances shall a Protective Home meant exclusively for victims be used as a place of penal detention or remand for perpetrators or organisers’. The bench of Acting Chief Justice Sam Koshy and Justice Narsing Rao Nandikonda gave these orders disposing of a writ petition filed by Prajwala, an NGO running a Protective Home, over rehabilitation of women and children rescued from traffickers and perpetrators of flesh trade.

The bench instructed the DGP to ensure coordination between different wings of police department over recruitment, grooming, coercion of women and children through social media, messaging applications, online advertisements, luring through placement offers. Police officers must be pro-active in identifying and preserving electronic records. “Any handling of devices or digital material shall preserve evidence related integrity and the privacy and dignity of victims, particularly children,”, the bench said.

There should not be any delay in referring complaints relating to online sexual exploitation, intimate images or suspected child sexual abuse material to the competent police officer or cybercrime official.
“Victims and families shall be informed of appropriate confidential reporting authorities and available protection,” the bench said.

The bench also directed the Education department officials to introduce age-appropriate awareness among children in each academic semester over recognising coercion, unsafe online contact, safe use of digital platforms and confidential access to teachers, counsellors and statutory reporting mechanisms. In colleges and universities, students should be explained about deceptive job and placement offers and exploitation through digital recruitment.

The bench instructed the Magistrates passing orders related to custody under section 17 of the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act-1956 to take precautions to prevent from placing genuine victims with the suspected exploiters in the same Preventive Home. It instructed the departments of Women and Child Development, Social Welfare, Health, Education and district administration to designate contact officers for coordination with the district Anti-Human Trafficking Units and District Legal Services Authorities.

articles.title: India’s Oct. crude import bill soars 87.5% to $19.5-bn amid West Asia tensions, volumes up 11%
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: While higher petroleum product exports offer a partial natural hedge, sustained increases in crude and gas prices could intensify pressure on the country’s import bill.

India’s crude oil import bill surged 87.5% year-on-year (YoY) to $19.5 billion in October, as elevated international benchmark prices, fuelled by renewed tensions in West Asia, sharply increased procurement costs. The increase came alongside an 11% rise in import volumes.

The net import bill, calculated as imports of crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas less exports of petroleum products, rose 60% to $16 billion during the month, compared with $10 billion in October last year.
Higher export realisations from petroleum products, however, provided some cushion against the escalating import burden.

According to provisional data released by the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC), India imported 23.3 million metric tonnes (MMT) of crude oil in October, against 21 MMT in the corresponding month last year.
The expenditure on crude imports, meanwhile, climbed to $19.5 billion from $10.4 billion, reflecting the disproportionate impact of higher international prices on the country’s energy import bill.

The Indian crude oil basket averaged $119.91 per barrel in October, compared with $124.77 per barrel for Brent crude. In September, the Indian basket had averaged $116.09 per barrel, while Brent stood at $116.77 per barrel.

The sustained increase in benchmark prices, amid continuing geopolitical uncertainties in West Asia, has left India exposed to higher energy procurement costs, given its dependence on imported crude oil.
The impact of the rising crude import bill was partly offset by stronger earnings from petroleum product exports.
India’s petroleum product exports increased 5.9% in volume terms to 5.4 MMT in October. However, export revenues surged approximately 91% to $6.3 billion.
The increase in export earnings provided an important buffer against the higher cost of crude procurement.

Meanwhile, India’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports declined approximately 7% to 3,014 million standard cubic metres (MMSCM) during October. Despite the decline in volumes, the import bill increased 8.33%, pointing to the persistence of price pressures in the international gas market.

articles.title: Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries for next U.S. House speaker
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Despite some opposition, Jeffries is expected to be elected speaker, a powerful position that puts him second in line to the Presidency, when the new Congress ‌convenes in early January

Democrats elected this month to the U.S. House ‌of Representatives nominated Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday (November 18, 2026) to lead them in the next Congress, putting him ‌on the precipice of becoming the nation's first ‌Black ⁠House speaker.
The incoming House Democratic Caucus nominated Mr. Jeffries ⁠in a closed-door, secret-ballot vote.

articles.title: Saudis prepare for Houthi war to last well into 2027
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Saudi and Yemeni forces are ​now reorganising, with plans to protect Aden from the Houthi advances and potentially shift their offensive to eastern fronts where they have made some advances or have at least held their lines

Saudi Arabia is preparing for war against Yemen's Houthis to stretch well into next year, doubling down despite setbacks on the battlefield in Yemen ​and attacks disrupting life at home, said two Western officials briefed by Saudis on the plans.

The renewed conflict has become the most active front in ‌the wider Iran war, killing and wounding thousands and displacing hundreds of thousands in Yemen while derailing ​Saudi Arabia's efforts to draw in non-oil investment and host global events.
Public messaging around the war has also ⁠slowly shifted in the kingdom, with greater acknowledgement of its impacts.

Saudi officials now foresee the campaign stretching on for up to six months, aiming to see gains on the ground by the kingdom's Yemeni allies before any negotiations with the Houthis, according to Western officials, who spoke on condition ‌of anonymity to discuss non-public conversations with Saudi counterparts.
A third source familiar with the Saudi plans confirmed the accounts. All three said a deal to end the wider Iran war could see the Yemen conflict draw down.

The ‌third source also said Riyadh believes that U.S. offensive support for Saudi operations in Yemen, which President Donald Trump's administration has ‌so ⁠far withheld, could help change the tide of the conflict, potentially allowing Saudi-backed forces to make the gains ⁠they want within weeks.
A Saudi Foreign Ministry official declined to comment on the views of Saudi officials as described by the Western officials.

Saudi Arabia first entered the Yemen conflict in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition to try to restore Yemen's government to power after the Houthis seized the ​capital Sanaa and much of the country. They fought to ‌a bloody stalemate and in 2022 reached a ceasefire that lasted until summer this year.

Since fighting restarted, the Houthis have seized the Red Sea coast and strategic Bab el-Mandeb strait from Saudi-backed forces, and encircled the city of Taiz in highlands above the government's temporary capital Aden on the southern coast.
Yemeni government forces mounted a counterattack last month, recapturing territory around the ‌strait, but withdrew over the past weekend to protect Aden in a major setback.

Saudi and Yemeni forces are ​now reorganising, with plans to protect Aden from the Houthi advances and potentially shift their offensive to eastern fronts where they have made some advances or have at least held their lines, according to one of the ⁠Western officials.

Saudi Arabia announced on Monday (November 16, 2026) it had replaced the commander overseeing the Saudi-led coalition. Yemen's government is also expected to reshuffle its military leadership, according to two people familiar with its plans.

articles.title: Ethiopia, Eritrea amass forces along border, heightening war fears: Sources
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: The fighting in Tigray has stoked fears of a ​wider conflagration in the Horn of Africa, with Ethiopia’s government also accusing Sudan, which is in the midst of its own civil war, and Egypt of backing the rebels; Eritrea, Sudan, Egypt ⁠all deny doing so

Ethiopia and Eritrea have amassed forces along their shared border, conflict monitors and people tied to militias in northern Ethiopia's Tigray ‌region said, fuelling fears of outright war between the historical rivals.

The build-up along the border has brought ​the two armies within striking distance of each other, according to the conflict monitors ACLED and the International ⁠Crisis Group, a person close to a pro-Ethiopian government militia in Tigray, and another person close to anti-government rebels there.

Reuters could not independently confirm reports of skirmishes between Ethiopian and Eritrean forces along the border. ACLED and a person close to the rebels said the ‌two sides had clashed in recent days, which would be their first direct armed exchanges in over a month, but the person close to the pro-Ethiopian government militia disputed this.

Reached for comment, Eritrean Information ‌Minister Yemane Gebremeskel decried "propaganda" from Ethiopia's ruling party about developments near the border but did not directly address reports about ‌military ⁠build-ups or clashes.
Spokespeople for the Ethiopian government did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Diplomats and ⁠experts have warned of possible conflict between Ethiopia and Eritrea since fighting broke out in September between Ethiopia’s federal government and rebels in Tigray, which borders Eritrea.

Witnesses and Ethiopia's government said Eritrean forces crossed into Tigray in early October in support ​of the rebels. ACLED reported at the time ‌that drone strikes it believed were carried out by Ethiopia’s military had targeted the Eritrean troops. Ethiopia has not commented on the strikes.

Eritrea has denied any incursion into Ethiopia and accused Addis Ababa of seeking a pretext to invade its smaller neighbour, which was an Ethiopian province for three decades before gaining independence in 1993. They are now separated ‌by a border stretching more than 1,000 km (620 miles).

The fighting in Tigray has stoked fears of a ​wider conflagration in the Horn of Africa, with Ethiopia’s government also accusing Sudan, which is in the midst of its own civil war, and Egypt of backing the rebels. Eritrea, Sudan, and Egypt ⁠all deny doing so.

Ethiopia and Eritrea fought a border war from 1998 to 2000 that killed tens of thousands of people. The conflict was prompted by a dispute over the border town of Badme, which a UN boundary commission later found fell within Eritrean ‌territory.

ACLED said in a statement late on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) that artillery shelling and armed clashes have occurred near Badme since last week as Ethiopia’s military moved to clear Tigrayan rebels from near the border.

It said that on November 12, Ethiopian drones targeted likely Eritrean positions around Badme and that Eritrean forces fired artillery toward Ethiopian positions. The next day, the two armies clashed on the Ethiopian side of the border, ACLED said.

articles.title: U.S.-Saudi nuclear agreement 'satisfactory': IAEA
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: According to the accord, the IAEA "will be provided with information about, and access to any sites for conversion, enrichment, fuel fabrication and reprocessing" in Saudi Arabia, Grossi said
UN nuclear watchdog head Rafael Grossi on Wednesday (November 18, 2026) welcomed a deal between the United States and Saudi Arabia on equipping the kingdom with a civilian nuclear programme.
The deal announced in July has provoked questions about the risks of nuclear proliferation.
"It's a very satisfactory outcome that we have with this agreement," Mr. Grossi told reporters after opening an International Atomic Energy Agency board of governors' meeting.
Once nuclear power development gets under way in Saudi Arabia, "we will be there," he added.

In his opening statement, Mr. Grossi told the board that the United States and Saudi Arabia in October requested the IAEA "to take the necessary steps to implement safeguards and verification measures" for their agreement.
According to the accord, the IAEA "will be provided with information about, and access to any sites for conversion, enrichment, fuel fabrication and reprocessing" in Saudi Arabia, Mr. Grossi said.
"I welcome the open, transparent approach and engagement of both governments with member states and the secretariat on this matter," he added.
Mr. Grossi told reporters the agreement was "fully aligned with the legal framework that we have at the IAEA".
He added Saudi Arabia had also agreed to "additional verification measures on a voluntary basis".
U.S. media have reported the agreement would allow Washington to export technology without the usual safeguards preventing future military use.
U.S. President Donald Trump said, just after the agreement was signed in July, that it depended on Saudi Arabia recognising Israel.

articles.title: India sitting on 'economic disaster': Rahul Gandhi at Columbia University
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: At Columbia University, Congress leader questions fairness of electoral process, speaks on manufacturing decline; links U.S. midterm setback to erosion of American power

Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi said the country’s economic model ceased to deliver results nearly a decade ago, leaving it with a deepening employment crisis and a weakened manufacturing base.

Speaking at a fireside chat at Columbia University on Tuesday (November 17, 2026), moderated by New York Times journalist Lydia Polgreen, Mr. Gandhi said India is sitting on an “economic disaster” that could become far more serious if the country continued on its present course.
“The blunt thing is that India is sitting on an economic disaster. That’s the reality of it,” he said.

“One can brush it aside, the media can brush it aside. But India has got a massive unemployment problem. India’s got a massive problem with its education system. And these are things you cannot get away from,” he added.

Mr. Gandhi identified small and medium businesses, agriculture and manufacturing as the backbone and principal engines of job creation, arguing that the services sector could not absorb India’s expanding workforce.

“The spine of the economy is small and medium business, which is the job creation engine, and agriculture. That is fundamental in India and required. The spine of the economy has been broken,” he said.

The Opposition leader said India could not achieve sustainable economic development without rebuilding its manufacturing capabilities. “We cannot survive successfully without manufacturing, it just cannot be done,” he said.
Mr. Gandhi alleged that economic growth was concentrated in a few large business groups while smaller enterprises were struggling.

“Why is there no private investment in India? Why are the only people who are growing in India, businesses that are growing in India called Adani and Ambani? Why is Tata literally being taken over by Mr. [Gautam] Adani?” he asked.

Mr. Gandhi placed the recent student-led Gen Z protests alongside resistance movements by Adivasis, Dalits and farmers against what he called the growing concentration of political and economic power in the last decade. He said the student-led protests showed that fear of “coercive power of the State” didn’t work.

“There’s a massive concentration of wealth taking place in India, and huge disenfranchisement of people. Vote is just one element of it,” he said, alleging that tribal land was being taken without consultation and that minorities, Dalits and farmers were facing growing marginalisation.

Referring to youth unemployment and economic difficulties in the U.S. and European countries, including Germany and Britain, Mr. Gandhi argued their economic challenges are serious and India’s relatively lower costs offer resilience, he said.

At Columbia University, Congress leader questions fairness of electoral process, speaks on manufacturing decline; links U.S. midterm setback to erosion of American power

Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi said the country’s economic model ceased to deliver results nearly a decade ago, leaving it with a deepening employment crisis and a weakened manufacturing base.

Speaking at a fireside chat at Columbia University on Tuesday (November 17, 2026), moderated by New York Times journalist Lydia Polgreen, Mr. Gandhi said India is sitting on an “economic disaster” that could become far more serious if the country continued on its present course.

“The blunt thing is that India is sitting on an economic disaster. That’s the reality of it,” he said.

“One can brush it aside, the media can brush it aside. But India has got a massive unemployment problem. India’s got a massive problem with its education system. And these are things you cannot get away from,” he added.

Mr. Gandhi identified small and medium businesses, agriculture and manufacturing as the backbone and principal engines of job creation, arguing that the services sector could not absorb India’s expanding workforce.

“The spine of the economy is small and medium business, which is the job creation engine, and agriculture. That is fundamental in India and required. The spine of the economy has been broken,” he said.

The Opposition leader said India could not achieve sustainable economic development without rebuilding its manufacturing capabilities. “We cannot survive successfully without manufacturing, it just cannot be done,” he said.

Mr. Gandhi alleged that economic growth was concentrated in a few large business groups while smaller enterprises were struggling.

“Why is there no private investment in India? Why are the only people who are growing in India, businesses that are growing in India called Adani and Ambani? Why is Tata literally being taken over by Mr. [Gautam] Adani?” he asked.

Mr. Gandhi placed the recent student-led Gen Z protests alongside resistance movements by Adivasis, Dalits and farmers against what he called the growing concentration of political and economic power in the last decade. He said the student-led protests showed that fear of “coercive power of the State” didn’t work.

“There’s a massive concentration of wealth taking place in India, and huge disenfranchisement of people. Vote is just one element of it,” he said, alleging that tribal land was being taken without consultation and that minorities, Dalits and farmers were facing growing marginalisation.

Referring to youth unemployment and economic difficulties in the U.S. and European countries, including Germany and Britain, Mr. Gandhi argued their economic challenges are serious and India’s relatively lower costs offer resilience, he said.

articles.title: UN Sustainable Development Goals group for science, technology rejigged
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: The group has been constituted even as the international community ramps up efforts to achieve the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development

The United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has reconstituted a 10-member group that works on promoting science, technology and innovation toward achieving its Sustainable Development Goals. The lone Indian in this group is former biologist and former Council of Scientific and Industrial Research CSIR Director General, Shekhar Mande, who is also currently President, Indian National Science Academy.
The group has been constituted even as the international community ramps up efforts to achieve the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, while preparing for the 2027 SDG Summit.

“The group comprises distinguished experts from diverse geographic and disciplinary backgrounds from both developing and developed countries. Each member, recognised for their international excellence in science or technology, brings a wealth of experience and insight from civil society, the private sector, and the scientific community, underscoring the inclusive and comprehensive approach the UN is taking towards sustainable development,” an accompanying press statement noted.

The other members of the group are Marian Dorcas Quain (Ghana), Deputy Director-General of CSIR Ghana; Giorgio Rossi (Italy), Vice-President of Elettra-Sincrotrone Trieste; Magnus Andersson (Sweden), Associate Professor at Malmö University; Mônica Tejo Cavalcanti (Brazil), Professor at the Federal University of Campina Grande; Evgeniya Dmitrieva (Russia), Member of the Civic Chamber of the Russian Federation; Motoko Kotani (Japan), Executive Director of Science at RIKEN; Jin Li (China), President of Fudan University; Madin Maseeh (Maldives), President of the Maldives Space Research Organisation; and Rita Orji (Nigeria), Canada Research Chair in Persuasive Technology at Dalhousie University.
Professor Mande is also President of Vijnana Bharti, which, along with the Ministry of Science and Technology is gearing up to host the India International Science Festival in Pune in December.

Announcing this on Wednesday (November 18, 2026), Union Minister of Science Jitendra Singh said at a press briefing that the government had taken a conscious decision to replace “scattered, repetitive gatherings”, including the erstwhile Indian Science Congress, with two flagship national events carrying distinct identities.

While the Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave in October saw 13 Ministries and Nobel Laureates, and was an academic-driven conclave exploring frontier themes, the India International Science Festival (IISF) brought a “festive, public-facing character with international resonance”. By rotating the venue to different regions, after Chandigarh, Hyderabad, Goa and Delhi, bringing IISF for the first time to Pune leverages the western hub’s vibrant academic, research, and industrial ecosystem.

articles.title: Bangladesh deploys paramilitary as unrest grows over Hasina's return
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Police have recorded dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of vehicles ​being torched in at least ‌28 districts over the last 10 days, with several police personnel and civilians injured, local media has reported

Bangladesh ‌stepped up security and deployed hundreds of paramilitary troops nationwide on Wednesday (November 18, 2026) ​as the planned return of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has ⁠sparked clashes, bomb blasts, and arson attacks blamed on supporters of her banned party.

Ms. Hasina, who has lived in exile in neighbouring India since she fled Dhaka following violent protests demanding ‌her resignation in August 2024, has requested a new passport and identity card, saying she plans to return in December.
But the government ‌has so far rejected her request, leading to members and supporters of ‌her ⁠Awami League party taking to the streets in protest.
Last week, the party ⁠announced a week-long programme of protests and rallies to mobilise support for Ms. Hasina's return, culminating in a nationwide lockdown on November 19.

Police have recorded dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of vehicles ​being torched in at least ‌28 districts over the last 10 days, with several police personnel and civilians injured, local media has reported.

Late on Tuesday (November 17, 2026), an activist of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) was allegedly killed by unidentified people during a protest ‌near Ms. Hasina's home district of Gopalganj, police said.

On the same night, a ​crude bomb exploded outside the Dhaka residence of Cultural Affairs Minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury, and the house of a BNP lawmaker and ⁠shops belonging to BNP supporters in Gopalganj were set on fire, police added.
On Wednesday (November 18, 2026) morning, a bus company helper was burnt to death in the southern district ‌of Pirojpur after two buses were set on fire, authorities said.

Tuesday (November 17, 2026) marked the day on which Ms. Hasina was sentenced to death a year ago by a local court that found her guilty of ordering a deadly crackdown on the student-led uprising against her in 2024.

At least 37 Grameen Bank branches and offices have been targeted in arson attacks or attempted fires ‌since November 10, with 14 more attacked since midnight on Tuesday (November 17, 2026), the bank said.
The bank was ​founded by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus, who led Bangladesh's interim government after Ms. Hasina's ouster and has faced hostility from Ms. Hasina's supporters.

Dhaka Metropolitan ⁠Police have arrested at least 71 members of banned organisations, including the Awami League ⁠and its affiliated outfits, in the last 24 hours, police spokesperson Niaz Mehedi said.

articles.title: Trump's Board of Peace faults Israel, Hamas for failure to end Gaza war
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: While the ceasefire has halted major fighting, the wider plan, which calls for Hamas ⁠to disarm, Israeli troops to withdraw and reconstruction to begin, has effectively stalled since soon after it came into effect last year

The body overseeing U.S. President Donald Trump's plan to end the Gaza ‌war accused both Israel and Hamas of failing to meet their commitments to end hostilities, leaving ​the population of Gaza in dire conditions and the ceasefire in danger of collapse.

The 12-page Board ⁠of Peace report, seen by Reuters , is the body's second to the United Nations Security Council since the U.S.-backed ceasefire came into effect 13 months ago. It offers a sobering assessment of progress made since then.
The Board, established and headed by Mr. Trump, is expected ‌to present the report's findings to a meeting of the council in New York at the end of November.

"The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains ‌the principal risk to the process," the report said, warning that "a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be ‌sustained ⁠indefinitely."

While the ceasefire has halted major fighting, the wider plan, which calls for Hamas ⁠to disarm, Israeli troops to withdraw and reconstruction to begin, has effectively stalled since soon after it came into effect last year.

Hamas agreed in July to a Board of Peace roadmap to surrender its weapons and transfer governance of Gaza to a civilian transitional authority, but Israel rejected ​the roadmap, saying it will not withdraw until Hamas ‌is dismantled.
Israel has carried out near-daily strikes on Gaza, while the report said Hamas fighters have also continued attacks on Israeli troops.
"Every day that Israel continues strikes against Hamas targets, it delays putting Hamas' agreement to the roadmap to the test," the report said.
"Meanwhile, Hamas militant activity continues, the commitment to cease all military activities has not ‌been met in full by the parties, and the population faces another winter in tents and rubble."

Senior Hamas ​official Basem Naim dismissed the report as "pure disinformation", accusing the Board of Peace of providing cover to Israel to evade its commitments under the plan to end the war and to ⁠continue its aggression in Gaza.
The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and a spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Gaza's population of more than 2 million Palestinians lives confined to around a third of ‌the coastal territory, mostly in makeshift tents and damaged buildings, under the control of Hamas fighters. Israel occupies two-thirds of Gaza that has been largely razed and depopulated.

articles.title: How AI could reshape global growth and productivity
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: A key expected impact of AI is an unprecedented rise in labour productivity, as its success as a technological revolution is premised on such an increase; what remains to be seen is how pervasive its impact will be across different sectors of the economy

Many have likened the artificial intelligence (AI) phenomenon to the inventions of the steam engine or internal combustion engine in the 18th and 19th centuries, respectively. Only time can tell whether AI is epochal of that kind. In this two-part piece, we discuss the possible impact it may have on the global economy as a whole.

A key impact of AI is considered to be an unprecedented rise in labour productivity. In fact, if there is one purpose AI is supposed to serve, it is enhancing labour productivity multifold. Since labour productivity is a key variable in this puzzle, consider what it constitutes of (Box 1) . It is a ratio of output and workers employed. Now this ratio can rise in three different ways — a rise in output for a given number of workers employed (rise in the numerator); a loss of jobs which leads to a fall in the denominator; more jobs are created, but the output rises faster than the jobs (while both the numerator and the denominator are rising, the numerator rises faster than the denominator).

articles.title: Brace for impact: On rising inflation and external factors
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: High inflation due to external factors could soon exacerbate economic pain

India’s much-hyped domestic economic resilience is set to be tested over the next few months as external factors start to impose inescapable pressures. A case in point is inflation. The latest data on retail inflation show that it crossed the Reserve Bank of India’s 6% upper comfort limit in October 2026. According to economists, this is likely to continue through the third quarter of this financial year, which means at least two more months of high inflation. Agricultural shortfalls brought on by a patchy and deficient monsoon have meant that food inflation rose sharply to 8.5% in October 2026. Elevated fuel prices meant that inflation in the transport category also rose sharply. What is worse is that high inflation is spreading to almost every aspect of a household’s day-to-day needs. In fact, the latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) data show that 10 of the 12 major categories saw inflation in October, hitting their highest levels recorded in the new series of the index. So, things such as clothing, footwear, housing, furnishings, and services such as healthcare, education, communication, recreation, and restaurant and hospitality are not only getting more expensive, but they are doing so at an accelerating rate. This would have been bad enough had wages been increasing in real terms. Yet, the latest research by Data for India on the country’s official wage statistics shows that, while nominal wages doubled from 2012 to 2024, they actually fell 4% over the same period after adjusting for inflation. And this is sharper for high-skilled and high-earning workers. Lower wage earners saw marginal increases over this period. While this is of some comfort, it is the higher wage earners that drive consumption in an economy. Real wage contraction for them, which is likely to have worsened in 2026, will hit consumption levels and private investment.

Further, there is strong evidence to suggest that the official inflation metrics are not capturing the full extent of rising prices. Data on cash with the public and UPI transactions show the value of both has been growing in double digits over the last year and more, significantly outpacing nominal GDP growth. This either suggests that the informal economy is far larger than earlier thought or, more likely, that inflation is well above what the official figures are being able to capture. Unfortunately, there are no real magic-wand fixes to this situation. Inflation is largely beyond the government’s control, and wage growth cannot happen overnight. The only way forward is to continue trying to spur sector-specific growth and warn people of the impending storm.

articles.title: Critical ban: On recycling of lithium-ion batteries
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: India needs to create an entire ecosystem for recycling of lithium-ion batteries

On November 10, the Directorate General of Foreign Trade banned the export of lithium-ion battery black mass by moving it from the “free” to the “prohibited” list of exports. Black mass is an intermediate product when spent batteries and factory scrap are shredded. It contains valuable lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese and graphite. The Commerce Ministry says the ban will ensure feedstock for domestic refiners, lift their capacity utilisation and draw investment. While the recycling of lead-acid batteries end-to-end is an established ecosystem and formalised, too, lithium-ion battery recycling is an emerging segment with only a few dozen licensed operators but has much potential given the scale of use of such batteries in EVs. While the ban will redirect supply, it will not automatically create a market and ecosystem. Just banning export without creating an entire ecosystem will only lead to dumping of lithium-ion batteries into landfills if the blackmass has no market. Blackmass production is a largely mechanical process but further downstream processing is more specialised chemical processing requiring larger investment and further policy support. If downstream units are online, their output can directly feed into indigenous lithium-ion battery manufacture.

India depends heavily on imports for critical minerals such as those used in battery inputs. Beyond working on supply aspects, the government must address the price gap to create a robust recycling market. Under the Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022, producers buy extended producer responsibility (EPR) certificates from recyclers but these are undervalued. Cheap certificates reward recycling on paper over investment in high-yield plants. A floor price that covers the full cost of recovery, with digital tracking, would fix that. Rare earths show how recycling remains a missed opportunity for India because of policy gaps. A smartphone can be up to 1% neodymium-iron-boron magnet by weight. That puts its rare earth content at about 3,000 parts per million, comparable to India’s monazite beach sands. Extracting it takes less energy than mining. A magnet separated from the phone is about 30% rare earth. Magnets make up as much as 3% of a hard drive, but are usable only if they are removed before the drive is shredded for data destruction. Yet the e-waste rules do not require rare earth separation. Rare earths need a separate EPR category, too. Payment by weight cannot be applied for rare earth minerals.

articles.title: In a dilemma: On Sheikh Hasina and India-Bangladesh ties
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: India must improve ties with Bangladesh, and protect Hasina

Bangladesh’s former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina now in exile in India, has set off speculation about her imminent return to Dhaka by submitting an application for a new Bangladeshi passport and national identity card this week. The application, made through the Bangladesh High Commission in Delhi, was dismissed by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s Foreign Affairs Adviser Humayun Kabir, who said that the government in Dhaka would not grant a passport to a “terrorist”, and would seek her return via the extradition agreement as a “prisoner transfer process” with India. Ms. Hasina has already announced that she plans to return to Bangladesh in December this year, as she did after her previous stay in India in exile from 1975-1981, after the brutal assassination of her father Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and nearly every other member of her family. However, the situation is considerably different now. This time, Ms. Hasina came to India in 2024 fleeing mobs of protestors that overthrew her government, and has since been convicted by a tribunal for ordering a crackdown on thousands of students, and sentenced to death. In interviews, including to The Hindu , Ms. Hasina says she hopes to return to Bangladesh to argue her case and rebuild her party, the Awami League, but that is hardly likely, given the anger against her amongst the polity, and bipartisan consensus to ban the Awami League from politics. Despite the harsh rhetoric it employs against her, the BNP government is unlikely to wish for her return, as it would have to begin execution proceedings against the 79-year-old former Prime Minister, with international opposition to such a move expected to be voluble. Not doing so would only strengthen its opposition party, the Jamaat-e-Islami, that has accused the Rahman government of soft-pedalling the issue. The government must also worry about possible protests and violence within the country in the event Ms. Hasina returns.

The situation puts the Modi government in a spot. Ever since Ms. Hasina announced plans to return, during a virtual press conference held in Delhi on August 5 this year, Delhi-Dhaka ties have been on a downslide. The government’s decision not to prevent Ms. Hasina from addressing the press, where she used the opportunity to soundly criticise PM Rahman, meant the abrupt cancellation of the Bangladesh PM’s visit. Next month, the Indo-Bangladesh Ganga Water treaty is set to expire, and talks on its extension have also become a casualty. Ms. Hasina has been an honoured guest in India, and the government cannot physically restrain her from taking the flight to Dhaka or travelling to the land border at Petrapole to cross over. Nor can it wash its hands of her situation once she crosses over. New Delhi must redouble its diplomatic efforts on improving bilateral ties while also ensuring Ms. Hasina’s welfare.

Editorial Context: In a dilemma: On Sheikh Hasina and India-Bangladesh ties. This editorial examines the institutional, constitutional, and administrative dimensions shaping public policy and governance in India.

Constitutional & Policy Analysis: A critical evaluation of recent executive and judicial developments highlights the need for transparent implementation, federal cooperation, and statutory accountability across central and state institutions.

articles.title: New deal: On COP31 and lofty climate goals
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Nations must deliver on past promises before committing to lofty climate goals

The 31st Conference of Parties (COP) began this week in Antalya, Türkiye. Hosted by Türkiye and negotiations presided over by Australia, the run-up to the gathering saw ministerial delegations visit Fiji and Tuvalu. This was to serve as a stark reminder of the purpose of COPs, namely that it was small island nations that are most vulnerable to warming from rising greenhouse gas emissions. However, the opening days have belied this sense of urgency. Prominent world leaders, even from the European countries who as a group champion the cause most vociferously, have chosen to skip the meet. The agenda and pre-summit expectations suggest that the main concerns this year are likely to be about delivering on existing commitments such as delivering $300 billion a year by 2035, which was decided at COP29 in Baku, as well as the COP30 call to triple the adaptation finance during that interval. However, deciding how these climate funds will practically flow has been deferred to COP32. The second global stocktake, a periodic check on progress under the Paris Agreement, begins at COP31, but the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has dithered on a timeline for the next reports that will serve as the scientific push to policy makers to accelerate efforts towards keeping a rise in temperatures below 2°C, and more ambitiously 1.5°C.

The previous edition of COP30 concluded without a formal roadmap away from fossil fuels — a step back from the COP28 consensus in Dubai. There is a voluntary roadmap ahead of COP31 but it is out of the formal negotiating text. In the background of the West Asia war, the withdrawal of the United States from the Paris Agreement and financial strain writ large over Europe, funds are a challenge as evidenced in the recent Loss and Damage fund approval to Nepal of $21 million when the ask is in billions. COP31 president, Murat Kurum has laid an electrification target, which is to raise electricity’s share from 23% of total energy consumption to 35% by 2035. India has already refused to sign such a pledge and insisted on predictable climate finance, technology transfer, and nationally determined approaches to climate mitigation. These negotiations have a character of their own and deliberating nations must strive to get nations to deliver on past promises rather than commit to new lofty targets.

articles.title: Plea in SC says ghost Form 7s haunt Mustafabad constituency during Delhi SIR
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The petition said persons declared dead were alive, while persons said to have shifted were found at home. Thirty-seven applications examined by the authorities were found to be false or fabricated.

Congress leader Ali Mehdi approached the Supreme Court on Monday alleging that Assembly Constituency-69 (AC-69) of Mustafabad is seeing a “substantial” amount of ghost Form 7s seeking deletion of voters in the ongoing Delhi SIR, and a crisis of electoral integrity is brewing.

The writ petition filed through advocate Shariq Ahmed, and highlighting multiple reports by The Hindu, said voters whose names feature for deletion on the grounds of death, absence and permanent shifting were found to be very much alive, present and staying put at their recorded addresses on the electoral roll.

The persons in whose names Form 7s have been filed for deletion of these voters deny having filed or signed on the applications. The petition alleged that ghost Form 7s seemed to have been filed by phantom objectors in the Mustafabad constituency.

“The integrity of an electoral roll is compromised not only when an ineligible name remains upon it. It is equally compromised when an eligible elector is removed from it on a fact which never existed or upon an objection which the supposed objector never made. The present record discloses the latter danger in its stark form,” the writ petition said.
It said persons declared dead were alive, while persons said to have shifted were found at home. Thirty-seven applications examined by the authorities were found to be false or fabricated.
“The existence of a genuine objector and the existence of a genuine ground for deletion — In Mustafabad, both are under serious doubt at the same time,” Mr. Ahmed submitted.

Section 22 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 requires the Electoral Registration Officer to be satisfied, after proper verification of the facts, before an entry can be corrected or deleted.

Rule 13(2) of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960 requires an objection to the proposed inclusion of a name or an application for deletion to be made in Form 7 and to be preferred by a person whose own name is included in the electoral roll.
Form 7 requires identification of the applicant, identification of the elector objected to, the particular ground for deletion and a declaration as to the truth of the particulars stated.
The guidelines accompanying the form place the onus of substantiating the ground upon the applicant.

“There must be an identifiable person who has actually invoked the statutory process and there must be a factual ground capable of sustaining the deletion sought. If either fails, the foundation of the objection fails,” the petition said.

The petition drew attention to an investigation by The Hindu which reported that 28 electors against whom deletion applications had been submitted were physically traced to the addresses at which they were enrolled.

articles.title: India's exports up 29.9% in October; trade deficit narrows to $20.09 billion
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: The growth in India’s merchandise exports in October, the fastest in five years and faster than import growth, indicates that volumes of exports are growing along with prices
India’s merchandise exports rose to an all-time high of $49.5 billion in October 2026, bringing down the country’s overall trade deficit, official data released on Friday showed.
While a large part of this growth was due to petroleum products, Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said diversification of exports to various locations helped improve the numbers.
India’s total exports, including goods and services, stood at $89.99 billion in October 2026, up nearly 30% from last October.
The overall trade deficit shrank from $25.1 billion last October to $20.1 billion year-on-year.

“In the month of October, the exports of merchandise exports have registered a new peak of $49.47 billion,” Mr. Agrawal said at a press briefing. “This is the highest-ever monthly merchandise export value, along with the highest monthly growth of 45.03% in the last five years.”
Merchandise imports rose to a record high of $89.35 billion in October 2026, up 16.5% YoY. Total imports stood at $110.1 billion, a 16.6% increase.

According to trade experts, goods exports growing faster than merchandise imports shows that while the rise in global prices contributed to the increase in the value of India’s exports, there was also an increase in the underlying export volumes.

“The particularly encouraging part of this growth is that this is not in any particular sector, this is not in any particular geography, it is broad-based across countries and regions,” Mr. Agrawal added. “43 of our 50 top export destinations posted positive growth in October 2026 as compared to 2025.”
The data show that India’s exports to 12 out of its top 20 export destinations grew by double digits or more.
Mr. Agrawal pointed out that India’s exports to its free trade agreement (FTA) partners had grown strongly.
One of the key areas of diversification has been the African continent, with exports to that region growing 44% in April-September 2026 to $31.4 billion.
Notably, India’s trade with West Asia is recovering as countries find alternate routes and ports other than those along the constrained Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Clear the path: On SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: India should use multilateral fora to advance bilateral cooperation

While maintaining its hard stance on cross-border terrorism, India has an opportunity to recognise that many of its other interests still merit sustained cooperation with Pakistan as the latter’s climate minister Musadik Masood Malik prepares to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi. India’s official position since the Pahalgam attack and the ensuing confrontations along the border is that terrorism and bilateral talks cannot coexist. A month later, Prime Minister Narendra Modi signalled that India’s relations with Pakistan would remain subordinate to its demands on cross-border terrorism by extending the condition to trade and water. South Asia is already one of the least economically integrated regions worldwide, with intra-regional trade at around 5%, and, as Chatham House has inferred, strained ties between India and its neighbours have created diplomatic vacuums that Beijing has taken advantage of through trilateral and regional groupings. Now, by inviting all SCO members to the national capital and participating in meetings ahead of the August 2027 Islamabad Summit, New Delhi has shown some maturity as a convening power. Islamabad is also being pragmatic in keeping channels open during its SCO chairmanship by participating in an initiative championed by Mr. Modi.

The pursuit of regionwide water security remains particularly fluid, with India seemingly overlooking the fact that it is upstream of Pakistan and Bangladesh and downstream of China. After India stopped sharing routine hydrological data of the Indus river and approved the Chenab-Beas link tunnel project, Mr. Malik fanned the flames saying Pakistan would “cut off those hands” seeking to restrict its share of the water. Yet China has now restricted the same data vis-à-vis the Brahmaputra while it builds the Medog mega-dam in Tibet. articles.title: Outlook outage: On Microsoft and dangers of centralising digital systems
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The dangers of centralising the internet’s architecture are now clear

Last week, Microsoft’s suite of productivity and email software, which businesses, governments, hospitals and a host of other organisations rely upon round-the-clock, abruptly stopped working globally , affecting tens of millions of people around the world. The company has cited a network upgrade gone awry as the root cause of the incident. Incidents such as the Microsoft 365 outage are a natural consequence of businesses and governments allowing key digital systems to become centralised all over the world. The internet remains, and was pioneered as, a network of networks. If one business’s networks went down, the reasoning went, others would not fall like dominos: everyone was, after all, connected to everyone else. But the economics have long been prohibitive, with dedicated servers and web-connected infrastructure infeasible for all but the largest businesses, with even those firms seeking the enticing cost savings from socialised infrastructure. That made sense: the internet made shared infrastructure more economical, allowing hardware and maintenance costs to be spread so far and wide that at a per-user level prices have been negligible. Competition among major cloud providers, the few that remain at Microsoft’s scale, have kept prices affordable for enterprise software for all shades of organisations.

Digital services have grown more sophisticated, and more deeply integrated into the economy as this centralisation unfolded. But the downside is that, regardless of the sophistication and professionalism of any company, mistakes happen, and the scale of these mistakes can quickly cascade over to the entire economy. There are societal and organisational lessons to be gleaned from these episodes. There is no such thing as a reliable vendor. Governments must also draw a cyber sovereignty lesson here that does not simply entail swapping a global vendor for a domestic one. It is the subversion of the internet’s architecture that is at the root of these incidents. Investing in resilience — and shielding critical operations from destabilising disruptions, no matter how improbable — should inform attitudes to digital systems. As a new generation of AI data centres is poised to supercharge the centralised systems of yesteryear, it is all the more imperative to mitigate even occasional vagaries of large systems.
